planting.note: Fall-sow onto lean, gravelly or clay soil in full sun and leave exposed to winter cold; established mats can also be divided and transplanted in early spring.

directions: Small-leaf pussytoes forms dense, silvery-woolly mats across the driest shortgrass flats and clay hillsides of the High Plains, spreading slowly outward each year by short stolons rather than seed. Because the species is dioecious, male and female plants look slightly different and only female colonies produce the papery, everlasting flower clusters in late spring. It thrives in lean, compacted, or rocky soil where most other groundcovers fail, and resents rich, moist beds that encourage rot. Use it between stepping stones, on a dry slope, or as a low-water turf substitute in a shortgrass-steppe planting.

planting.note: Direct sow after scarifying the hard seed coat, since this species forms a deep woody taproot early and transplants poorly once established.

directions: Narrowleaf four o'clock is a bushy, deep-rooted shortgrass and mixed-grass prairie native with slender, grass-like leaves and small magenta-pink trumpet flowers that open in late afternoon and close by mid-morning. Its thick, carrot-like taproot lets it resprout reliably from drought, grazing, or fire, which is why direct seeding in place works far better than attempting to move started plants. Evening-flying moths and other dusk pollinators visit the blooms through summer, making it a worthwhile addition to a late-day pollinator planting. Give it the leanest, driest, sunniest spot available and skip supplemental watering once it is through its first season.

planting.note: Fall-sow into lean, rocky or clay soil and let winter cold break dormancy; germination is slow and uneven without a cold period.

directions: Spreading buckwheat is a low, woody-based subshrub scattered across the clay and shale breaks of the central High Plains, forming a loose mound of gray-green leaves topped by branched sprays of small cream flowers that age to rust through summer. It is an important late-season nectar source for native bees and butterflies on sites too dry and exposed for most other flowering plants. Once its deep root system is established it needs no irrigation and resents heavy or regularly watered soil. Plant it on a gravel bank, dry border, or shortgrass-steppe restoration where its understated color works well against grasses like blue grama.

planting.note: Nick or sand the hard seed coat and fall-sow directly where plants are to grow; the long taproot rarely survives transplanting from containers.

directions: Missouri milkvetch hugs the ground in low, silvery-haired mounds on the driest shortgrass and gravel benches of the High Plains, sending up showy magenta-purple pea flowers in very early spring before most other prairie forbs have started growth. The blooms are followed by inflated, papery, silver-mottled seedpods that add a second season of interest and help distinguish it from other regional milkvetches. Like most Astragalus species it carries a single deep taproot and depends on root-associated bacteria for nitrogen, so avoid fertilizing or overwatering, both of which shorten its life. It suits a gravel bed, rock garden, or unirrigated native planting where its early bloom and low profile won't be shaded out by taller neighbors.

planting.note: Fall-sow onto lean, well-drained prairie soil and leave exposed to winter cold; plants typically flower from a basal rosette the following spring.

directions: Largeflower Townsendia grows as a short-lived rosette plant across the shortgrass and mixed-grass High Plains, producing lavender-blue daisy flowers noticeably larger than those of its low, stemless relative the Easter daisy. It typically behaves as a biennial or short-lived perennial, flowering heavily in its second year and reseeding itself readily on open, undisturbed ground. Give it the same lean, sharply drained, mineral-rich soil it uses in the wild, since rich garden beds encourage soft growth and rot. It is an excellent early-season choice for a gravel bed, dry border edge, or shortgrass restoration planting where self-sown seedlings can be allowed to fill in gaps.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring into sandy or gravelly, fast-draining soil; this short-lived species reseeds itself readily once established in open ground.

directions: Spectacle pod is a quirky mustard-family native of the sandy and gravelly shortgrass flats of the southern High Plains and Texas-Oklahoma Panhandle, named for its distinctive two-lobed, inflated seedpods that look remarkably like a pair of old-fashioned spectacles once the spring flush of small white flowers fades. Plants behave as short-lived annuals or biennials, forming a basal rosette of lobed gray-green leaves before bolting into a loosely branched flowering stem. It thrives in disturbed, open, poor soil and is easily grown from direct-sown seed, often naturalizing into a self-sustaining colony along a dry path or gravel bed. Leave some seedpods standing through summer, since the dried pods are as much a conversation piece in dried arrangements as the flowers are in the garden.
